verdict.rationale: Three lexical threads converge across the canon. First, Gen 1:27 predicates the divine tselem (H6754) of ha-adam as a category without developmental qualifier, and Gen 9:6 grounds the inviolability of human blood (dam ha-adam, H1818 + H0120) in that same image (ki betselem elohim asah eth ha-adam), with the verbal repetition shofek dam ha-adam ba-adam damo yishshafek (H8210 chiasm) making the image the explicit ratio of the prohibition. Second, the murder prohibition lo tirtsach (Exod 20:13 and Deut 5:17, H3808 plus H7523) uses ratsach, which Num 35:16-25 reserves for the unlawful killer over against the judicial executor (H4191 hiphil) and the wartime killer (H2026, harag), tightening its denotation to unlawful killing of an innocent human person, the very category Exod 23:7 and Prov 6:17 mark as forbidden under the rubric dam naqi (innocent blood). Third, the womb texts use continuous personal grammar across the prenatal stage: Ps 139:13-16 carries first-person verbs and suffixes through formation while the speaker is still golem (H1564, a true hapax), Jer 1:5 places yada (H3045), yatsar (H3335), and qadash (H6942) before formation in the beten (H0990) with second-person object suffixes, Isa 49:1,5 doubles the pattern with mibbeten and yatsar, Hos 9:11 even names the triad birth, womb, conception (herayon, H2032), and Luke 1:41,44 calls the unborn John brephos (G1025), the identical noun used of the newborn Jesus and of nursing infants in Luke 2:12, 2:16, 18:15, with sole occurrence-set spanning in-utero and post-utero usage. The Exod 21:22-25 crux is ambiguous in Hebrew but on a careful read of yatsa (the verb of normal birth in Jer 1:5) and ason (calamity, not specifying mother or child) the law is consistent with rather than against the broader pattern, so it does not lower confidence below high.

scripture.force: וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים בָּרָא אֹתוֹ זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם. The threefold bara with the human as object, and the prepositional bətselem (in the image), predicates the divine image of ha-adam as such without restriction by developmental stage, sex, or capacity. Gen 1:27 defines the category of the human as image-bearer, the value-grounding premise the sanctity claim depends on, and the same noun adam is the one whose blood Gen 9:6 protects.

שֹׁפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם דָּמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם. The chiastic shafak-dam-adam-adam-damo-yishshafek frame makes human blood inviolable, and the causal ki betselem elohim asah eth ha-adam supplies the explicit ratio: the image of God in adam is the ground of the prohibition. This single verse fuses the two anchor lemmas (tselem and dam) that the rest of the canon develops, and it predicates the image of the human category (not of any subset by age or stage).

לֹא תִּרְצָח. The negated imperfect of ratsach is an absolute prohibition. The Pentateuchal pattern (Num 35:16-25) reserves ratsach for the unlawful killer (the murderer and the manslayer, both designated rotseach), over against H4191 hiphil for judicial execution (Num 35:30, 35:31) and H2026 harag for general or wartime killing. So ratsach denotes precisely the unlawful taking of an innocent human person, which is the moral category the proposition addresses. Deut 5:17 repeats the same prohibition verbatim, confirming canon-stable usage.

לֹא תִּרְצָח. Verbatim repetition of Exod 20:13 in the Deuteronomic rehearsal of the Decalogue, establishing the ratsach prohibition as pan-Pentateuchal and not localized to a single context. Two independent witnesses to the same lexical choice.

כָּל מַכֵּה נֶפֶשׁ לְפִי עֵדִים יִרְצַח אֶת הָרֹצֵחַ. In a single verse ratsach is used both for the act being judicially punished and (with the participle rotseach) for the agent of unlawful killing, while the judicial putting-to-death uses H4191 hiphil. The lexical contrast between ratsach (unlawful killing) and muth-hiphil (judicial execution) is grammatically explicit here, foreclosing the reading that Exod 20:13 forbids all killing.

וְנָקִי וְצַדִּיק אַל תַּהֲרֹג. The jussive of harag governs the explicit object naqi (innocent) plus tsaddiq (righteous), categorically forbidding the killing of the innocent person. This generalizes the ratsach prohibition to the broader semantic field and explicitly names innocence as the protected category, the same category the womb texts establish for the unborn.

אַתָּה קָנִיתָ כִלְיֹתָי תְּסֻכֵּנִי בְּבֶטֶן אִמִּי. God is subject of qanah (acquire, form) and sakak (weave, cover) acting on the first-person speaker bəbeten (in the womb). The prenatal subject is referred to by the same personal pronoun and suffix that the psalmist uses of his present adult self, with no lexical break between the womb stage and present personhood.

נוֹרָאוֹת נִפְלֵיתִי וְנַפְשִׁי יֹדַעַת מְאֹד. The niphal of palah predicates that the speaker was wondrously distinguished in formation, and the personal nefesh carries continuous knowledge through the formation narrative. The same I that speaks now is the I that was being made.

לֹא נִכְחַד עָצְמִי מִמֶּךָּ אֲשֶׁר עֻשֵּׂיתִי בַסֵּתֶר רֻקַּמְתִּי. The pual ruqamti (I was intricately woven, raqam) describes the speaker as the woven object in the hidden place, the womb figured as the depths of the earth. The first-person verb assigns the developing body to the continuous I of the speaker, and raqam itself is rare (9 occurrences, all elsewhere of woven tabernacle and priestly textile work) so its application to embryology is striking and deliberate.

גָּלְמִי רָאוּ עֵינֶיךָ וְעַל סִפְרְךָ כֻּלָּם יִכָּתֵבוּ יָמִים יֻצָּרוּ. God sees the golem, the unformed embryonic mass, which is a true hapax legomenon (a single occurrence in the canon, only here), and the days are written before any of them existed. The verse predicates divine perception and ordained continuity of the same individual from the unformed stage onward. Because golem occurs only here, its sense rests on the parallelism: it is what is woven in the womb and seen by God, that is, the prenatal human under formation. This is the strongest single-verse witness to prenatal personal identity.

בְּטֶרֶם אֶצּוֹרְךָ בַבֶּטֶן יְדַעְתִּיךָ וּבְטֶרֶם תֵּצֵא מֵרֶחֶם הִקְדַּשְׁתִּיךָ. The double bəterem (before) places yada (know, with personal object suffix), yatsar (form in the womb), and qadash (set apart) on a timeline that begins before formation. All four verbs carry the second-person suffix, treating the prenatal Jeremiah as the same addressee God commissions. The collocation yatsar plus beten plus terem also occurs in Isa 44:2 and Isa 49:5 of the Servant, showing the womb-shaping pattern is canon-wide and not a one-off poetic flourish.

יְהוָה מִבֶּטֶן קְרָאָנִי מִמְּעֵי אִמִּי הִזְכִּיר שְׁמִי. The Servant says the LORD called him from the womb (mibbeten) and named him from the inward parts (mimme'e) of his mother. The grammar places a divine speech-act (qara, call) and a divine naming on the prenatal subject. This is a second prophetic witness, independent of Jer 1:5, to personal address and identity prior to birth.

יוֹצְרִי מִבֶּטֶן לְעֶבֶד לוֹ. The participle yotsri (my Former) plus mibbeten (from the womb) plus the purpose le'eved (to be a servant) directly mirrors Jer 1:5 and confirms that yatsar (the verb of divine forming) operates lexically within the womb stage, not merely on the post-natal person. Two prophetic books, one identical lexical pattern.

מִלֵּדָה וּמִבֶּטֶן וּמֵהֵרָיוֹן. The triad birth, womb, conception. Herayon is exceedingly rare (only 3 occurrences, here and Gen 3:16 and Ruth 4:13). The lexical pattern names a continuous human existence whose loss is grievous at each of the three stages, including conception. This is the closest single-clause witness to a from-conception lexical frame in the Hebrew canon.

ἐσκίρτησεν τὸ βρέφος ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ αὐτῆς. The unborn John is called brephos, the identical noun Luke applies to the just-born Jesus in the manger (Luke 2:12, 2:16) and to nursing infants brought to Jesus (Luke 18:15), and which Acts 7:19 uses of newborn Hebrew babies and 2 Tim 3:15 of Timothy from infancy and 1 Pet 2:2 of newborn babes longing for milk. All 8 canonical occurrences of brephos cluster as one set, with no separate term for the unborn. skirtao (leap) predicates volitional response to Mary's greeting. The lexical choice assigns the in-utero child the same person-noun as a delivered infant.

ἐσκίρτησεν ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει τὸ βρέφος ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ μου. Elizabeth attributes agalliasis (exultation, joy) to the brephos, predicating an inner affective state of the unborn child. The grammar treats prenatal John as a personal subject capable of joy, not a pre-personal tissue stage. skirtao occurs only 3 times in the NT canon (here, Luke 1:41, and Luke 6:23 of disciples leaping for joy), so its sole non-prenatal use is of mature personal joy, transferring that connotation to the womb scene.

יָדַיִם שֹׁפְכוֹת דָּם נָקִי. Hands that shed innocent blood (dam naqi) are listed among the things YHWH hates, the toebah of v. 16. The construct dam naqi designates blood that is guiltless, marking the killing of the innocent as the specific object of divine hatred and abomination, which supplies the moral-category force the proposition asserts (not liberty, but toebah).

וַיִּשְׁפְּכוּ דָם נָקִי דַּם בְּנֵיהֶם וּבְנוֹתֵיהֶם אֲשֶׁר זִבְּחוּ לַעֲצַבֵּי כְנָעַן. Israel's child-sacrifice is described with the same shafak dam naqi locution as Prov 6:17 and Deut 19:10, and the children sacrificed are explicitly called sons and daughters (bənehem ubənothehem). The verse fuses three threads: shed innocent blood, applied to children, with the result that the land is polluted (chanaph) by dam. This is the closest canonical analogue in lexical terms to the killing of children as a religious or social act, and it is condemned categorically.

וְלֹא יִשָּׁפֵךְ דָּם נָקִי בְּקֶרֶב אַרְצְךָ. The cities-of-refuge legislation explicitly invokes shafak plus dam naqi as the harm to be prevented, confirming that dam naqi (innocent blood) is a fixed legal-moral category across the Pentateuch, not a poetic flourish in Proverbs alone.

complicating_texts.resolution: This is the historical lexical crux. The clause says if men strive and strike a pregnant woman and her children come out (וְיָצְאוּ יְלָדֶיהָ, yatsa with plural yeladim as subject), and there is no ason (אָסוֹן, calamity), the offender pays a fine determined by the woman's husband. If there is ason, then nefesh tachat nefesh, life for life. The lexical question is the referent of ason. One reading takes yatsa as miscarriage and the no-ason case as a property-style fine, implying the fetus has reduced status. The competing reading observes that yatsa is the standard verb of normal birth (Jer 1:5 tetse merechem, Gen 25:25-26 of Esau and Jacob coming out, Job 1:21 of coming out of the mother's belly) and never elsewhere denotes miscarriage, for which the Hebrew uses shakal (H7921) or nefel (H5309, as in Job 3:16 and Eccl 6:3). On the second reading the law describes premature live birth, with ason then covering injury or death to either mother or child, in which case the lex talionis explicitly protects the unborn. The plural yeladim as subject also fits live birth more naturally than miscarriage. Because yatsa-merechem language is used positively of personal subjects elsewhere in the canon (the same root and stem appears in Jer 1:5 of the prophet emerging), the second reading is lexically the stronger one. Either way, the passage cannot bear the weight of overturning the broader image-and-womb pattern, since it stands alone and its key term ason is unspecified for subject. So it complicates but does not reverse the verdict.

The נֵפֶל (nefel, stillbirth, H5309) is said to have better rest than a long-lived but unsatisfied man. The verse is a comparative wisdom hyperbole about the futility of a joyless long life, not a statement about the ontological status of the fetus. It still grants the nefel a comparative experiential frame (rest, menuchah), and Job 3:16 uses nefel similarly. Hyperbolic comparative wisdom genre does not negate the personal-subject lexemes of Ps 139 and Jer 1:5.

The Midianite war command to kill male children and non-virgin women is sometimes invoked against the broad innocent-blood category. But the Hebrew uses harag (H2026, the wartime kill verb) and the context is the herem of a specific judicial-prophetic war, not the absolute ratsach prohibition of Exod 20:13. The lexical distinction between ratsach (unlawful innocent killing) and harag (general or wartime killing under specific command) is exactly what Num 35 establishes, so this text does not lexically conflict with the sanctity claim, it confirms the very semantic boundary on which it rests.

variants.note: The decisive anchor texts (Gen 1:27, Gen 9:6, Exod 20:13, Deut 5:17, Num 35:30, Ps 139:13-16, Jer 1:5, Isa 49:1,5, Hos 9:11, Prov 6:17, Ps 106:38, Deut 19:10) are Hebrew and outside ECM scope. The Greek anchor Luke 1:41-44 carries no load-bearing variant affecting βρέφος, σκιρτάω, or ἀγαλλίασις. NA28, SBLGNT, and Nestle1904 agree on the substantive readings of the Lukan passage. The brephos identification of the unborn John is textually stable.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: The unborn is the same personal subject as the later-born individual and bears the divine image, so the murder prohibition applies and the intentional killing of the innocent unborn falls under ratsach and shafak-dam-naqi.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Ps 139, Jer 1:5, Isa 49:1,5, Hos 9:11, and Luke 1:41-44 carry first and second-person verbs and suffixes continuously across the womb stage, and the rare hapax golem in Ps 139:16 attaches divine sight and ordained continuity to the unformed embryo. Luke 1:41 uses the in-canon noun brephos for the unborn John, the same noun used of post-natal infants in Luke 2:12, 2:16, 18:15 and Acts 7:19, with no separate term for the unborn. Gen 9:6 grounds the inviolability of human blood in the divine image with explicit causal ki betselem elohim, and Exod 20:13 plus Num 35:30 distinguish ratsach (unlawful killing) from judicial execution. The lexical continuity admits no caesura between prenatal and postnatal identity, and the prohibition operates on the human category as such.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: Full nefesh status is reached incrementally, so the womb texts are devotional or election language rather than statements of full personhood at conception, and early prenatal loss is a lesser harm.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: This lens leans primarily on Exod 21:22 read as a fine for fetal loss (treating yatsa as miscarriage and ason as harm to the mother alone), and on the poetic genre of Ps 139 to soften the personhood inference. It also notes that nephesh in Gen 2:7 attaches at the in-breathing of life. Stated in its strongest form, it grants that the unborn is a developing human under divine care but reserves the full ratsach prohibition for the post-natal person, treating early loss as a serious but lesser category. It is lexically possible for Exod 21:22 in isolation but it must (a) read yatsa against its uniform canonical use of normal birth and (b) discount the consistent personal-subject grammar of Jer 1:5 and the Lukan brephos equation, so it survives only by privileging one ambiguous legal text over the wider canon pattern.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: Because the human bears the divine image, the ratsach prohibition guards human life as a sacred category, and shedding innocent blood is a toebah, an abomination, not a matter of liberty.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Gen 1:27 plus Gen 9:6 plus Exod 20:13 plus Prov 6:17 plus Ps 106:38 combine to make the unlawful killing of an innocent image-bearer categorically condemned. The moral force is lexically anchored in ratsach (unlawful killing), dam naqi (innocent blood), toebah (abomination), and the explicit ki betselem elohim of Gen 9:6, not merely inferred. The image is predicated of ha-adam without developmental qualifier in the verses that ground the prohibition.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: The womb-knit passages speak primarily of God's electing call on specific covenant figures (Jeremiah, the Servant, John the Baptist, Paul), and the general personhood-of-the-unborn extension is a secondary inference.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Stated in its strongest form, Jer 1:5, Isa 49:1,5, Luke 1:15-44, and Gal 1:15 are commissioning narratives about chosen vessels, not universal anthropology. However, the underlying lexical verbs yatsar, yada, qadash, and qara are not restricted in their canonical usage to elect figures (yatsar of all humans in Ps 33:15 and yada of humans broadly), and Ps 139 is generalized first-person reflection, not a commissioning narrative. So this lens validly cautions against over-reading commissioning texts but does not displace the broader personhood lexemes of Ps 139, Gen 1:27, and Luke 1:41 (which uses brephos, not a commissioning verb).

hermeneutics.notes: The lexical pattern strongly supports prenatal personal identity (Ps 139, Jer 1:5, Isa 49:1,5, Hos 9:11, Luke 1:41-44), grounds it in image-bearing of the human category (Gen 1:27, Gen 9:6), and lexically distinguishes ratsach (the unlawful killing of an innocent person) from judicial execution and wartime killing (Num 35:30, Exod 23:7). Shafak dam naqi (Prov 6:17, Deut 19:10, Ps 106:38) marks killing the innocent as toebah. The one materially contested point is the Exod 21:22-25 crux. A close lexical reading of yatsa-from-the-womb (consistently positive in the canon) and the unspecified subject of ason resolves the crux in favor of, not against, sanctity, but even on the gradualist reading the single ambiguous legal text cannot outweigh the broader image-and-womb pattern.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Does the canon use personal, individuated, image-bearing language for the human from the prenatal stage, and does the prohibition rendered lo tirtsach (with ratsach distinguished from harag and muth-hiphil) cover the unlawful taking of innocent human life such that the lexical data bear on whether intentionally ending the life of the innocent unborn falls under that prohibition.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem preloads the moral verdict with the phrases is sin under the sixth commandment and not a morally neutral matter or a matter of Christian liberty. These are normative conclusions, not lexemes. The neutralized form isolates the answerable lexical questions: image-of-God predication on the human category, prenatal personhood grammar across the canon, the semantic range of ratsach, and the canonical force of shafak-dam-naqi. The verdict was derived on the original stem but the lexical inquiry was run on the neutral questions. The deepened query (canon-distribution checks of H6754, H7523, H1818, H5355, H1564, H2032, G1025, plus full morphology of Gen 9:6, Num 35:16-25, Exod 21:22-25, Deut 19:10, Ps 106:38, Isa 49:1,5, Hos 9:11) raised confidence from medium to high by showing (1) the ratsach vs harag vs muth-hiphil distinction is grammatically explicit in Num 35 itself, foreclosing the all-killing reading of Exod 20:13, (2) Gen 9:6 supplies the explicit causal link ki betselem elohim that the prior file noted only implicitly, (3) the womb-and-formation pattern is canon-wide (Jer 1:5, Isa 49:1,5, Hos 9:11 with herayon naming conception, Ps 139 with the hapax golem) rather than dependent on one psalm, (4) the dam-naqi locution is fixed legal language (Deut 19:10, Ps 106:38, Prov 6:17), and (5) yatsa in Exod 21:22 lexically aligns with normal birth elsewhere, weakening the strongest counter-text. The morally-neutral clause survives at high confidence on the canon pattern. The verdict still affirms; the standing affirm is preserved.

lay_summary: Several Hebrew and Greek word patterns bear on this proposition and they converge from different angles. Genesis 1:27 predicates the divine image (tselem) of the human (adam) as a category, with no qualifier for stage of life. Genesis 9:6 then says that whoever sheds the blood of a human, by a human shall his blood be shed, with the explicit reason: for in the image of God He made the human. The image of God is the stated ground of the prohibition on shedding human blood. Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17 both read lo tirtsach, do not murder, using the verb ratsach. Numbers 35:30 shows ratsach used for the unlawful killer while judicial execution uses a different verb, and Exodus 23:7 explicitly forbids killing the innocent person with naqi (innocent) and tsaddiq (righteous) named as the protected object. So ratsach denotes precisely the unlawful taking of an innocent human life. The womb passages use personal, individuated grammar. Psalm 139:13 to 16 has God forming, weaving, and acquiring the speaker in the womb, with the same first-person pronouns the psalmist uses of his present adult self, and God sees the golem, the unformed embryonic mass, which is a hapax legomenon, a word appearing only here in the Hebrew canon. Jeremiah 1:5 places know, form, and set apart before formation in the womb, all carrying a personal object suffix. Isaiah 49:1 and 49:5 repeat the same pattern of calling and forming from the womb. Hosea 9:11 names the triad birth, womb, and conception (herayon, used only three times in the canon), the closest single-clause witness to a from-conception lexical frame. Luke 1:41 to 44 calls the unborn John a brephos, the very same noun Luke uses of the newborn Jesus in the manger and of nursing infants, and attributes leaping and joy to him. Proverbs 6:17, Deuteronomy 19:10, and Psalm 106:38 all use the fixed locution shafak dam naqi, shed innocent blood, with Psalm 106:38 applying it explicitly to children sacrificed by their parents. One legal text, Exodus 21:22 to 25, is grammatically ambiguous and historically the strongest counter-anchor. The verb yatsa, come out, is the same root used elsewhere of normal birth (including Jeremiah 1:5 itself), and the noun ason, calamity, does not specify whose calamity is in view. So the text plausibly describes premature live birth with the life-for-life clause protecting the child too. Across all these threads the lexical pattern treats the unborn as a known, formed, image-bearing human and treats the unlawful killing of the innocent as categorically condemned. Legitimate distinctions the words themselves preserve are self-defense and judicial execution (a different verb), wartime killing under specific command (a different verb), and natural miscarriage (a different vocabulary, nefel or shakal). The case is strong because it does not depend on any one verse but on a recurring lexical structure across narrative, law, wisdom, prophecy, and gospel.
